tagline: Mountain roads pass a marble courthouse, a gorge and roadside waterfalls.
intro: The Waterfall Byway winds through five western North Carolina counties, linking Murphy and Rosman by way of mountain forests, the Cullasaja Gorge and roadside waterfalls. NCDOT includes it in the state’s scenic byways and gives the 98-mile drive a time of two hours and thirty minutes. US 64 bends past blind curves at Cullasaja Falls and crosses Cowee Gap at a sharp switchback.

The highway’s western reaches have changed course as the region changed. Construction of US 64 between Hayesville, Warne and Brasstown began in 1921, and the connection from Hayesville to Franklin followed in the early 1930s. Building Chatuge Dam and its reservoir required relocating part of US 64, along with 278 families and 532 graves. The dam’s gates closed in February 1942. In 1959, a new highway from Hayesville through Sweetwater to Peachtree took the US 64 number; the former route became Old Highway 64.

Traveling east from Murphy, the main byway goes through Brasstown before joining US 64 toward Chatuge Lake and Franklin. Continue through the Cullasaja Gorge, passing Dry Falls and Bridal Veil Falls on the way to Highlands. Beyond Highlands come Cashiers, Sapphire Valley and the crossing over Toxaway Falls, before the route ends just west of Rosman.

moments.title: Murphy
moments.text: Blue marble faces Murphy’s Cherokee County Courthouse, a material chosen after three courthouse fires. The previous brick courthouse burned in 1895, was restored and reopened in 1896, then burned again in January 1926. For its replacement, commissioners used blue marble from the Regal quarry in Marble, less than ten miles away. Dedicated in November 1927, the courthouse has a four-columned Corinthian portico and a cupola. The 2013 expansion used different exterior materials because the original quarry had closed. Inside, the floors are marble, and the courtroom retains much of its original woodwork and stone detailing.

moments.title: Bridal Veil Falls
moments.text: US 64 once sent every vehicle behind Bridal Veil Falls, using the curve tucked under its overhanging bluff. Ice on that roadway during freezing weather caused problems, so the highway was rerouted in front of the waterfall. The 45-foot falls flow on a tributary of the Cullasaja River in Nantahala National Forest. In 2003, a fallen boulder blocked one side of the old drive-under; a local developer removed it in July 2007. The old curve is now pedestrian-only. During drought the stream can nearly dry up; moderate or high flow wets visitors behind the falls.

moments.title: Highlands
moments.text: Highlands began with two lines drawn across a map. Samuel Truman Kelsey and Clinton Carter Hutchinson connected Chicago with Savannah and New Orleans with New York, expecting their intersection to become a trading center. They founded the town in 1875 on a southern Appalachian plateau. Its official average elevation within town limits is 4,118 feet. The roads connect the town with the surrounding terrain: US 64 toward Franklin follows the Cullasaja River, while the road toward Cashiers offers views of Whiteside Mountain. Between Highlands and Cashiers, US 64 crosses the Eastern Continental Divide at Cowee Gap.

practical: Bridal Veil Falls: The road behind Bridal Veil Falls is closed to vehicles and used for pedestrian access only. (checked 2026-10-11)
Highlands: NCDOT’s 2021 byways guide prohibits tractor-trailers on this route and does not recommend it for recreational vehicles or buses. (checked 2026-10-11)
